PulsarSubscription::pattern reads every topic whose full name matches a regular expression, topics created later included. The expression is matched against the full name of each topic, so it is written in full: persistent://public/default/orders-.*. The client lists one namespace for it, the one the prefix names: persistent://acme/orders/.* reads acme/orders, and a pattern with no tenant/namespace/ part reads public/default. The client lists the topics again every 30 seconds and joins the subscription to each new match. A topic created after startup is read from the listing that finds it on, and what reached it before that listing is not delivered. A pattern has no single topic to name the subscription by, so it reports under the subscription's own name. The expression is checked at startup, and one that is not a valid regular expression, or whose tenant or namespace is itself a regular expression, stops the service before any call to the server. The settings and their defaults are those of PulsarSubscription, and a seek moves the cursor on every topic the pattern reads. Topics and subscriptions audits every regional order topic, those created later included.

Every orders-* topic is recorded byte for byte, whatever its producer wrote; returns is not. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_pattern.rs /// What the `orders-*` producers write is not one schema, so the payload rides the byte lane: /// `Deserialized` names the bytes without decoding them. #[derive(Deserialized)] struct Record<'a>(&'a [u8]); /// Records every `orders-*` topic of `public/default`, those created after startup included. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::pattern("persistent://public/default/orders-.*", "audit"))] async fn audit(record: &Record<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(bytes = record.0.len(), "order event recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/pulsar_pattern.rs /// What the `orders-*` producers write is not one schema, so the payload rides the byte lane: /// the type is built from the bytes as they arrived, and no codec runs. struct Record<'a>(&'a [u8]); impl Deserialized for Record<'_> { type Output<'a> = Record<'a>; type Error = Infallible; fn from_payload(payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Record<'_>, Infallible> { Ok(Record(payload)) } } impl Input for Record<'_> { type Axis = SoloDeserialized<Record<'static>>; } /// Records each event of those topics. struct Audit; impl Handle<Record<'_>> for Audit { fn handle( &self, record: &Record<'_>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(bytes = record.0.len(), "order event recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // Every `orders-*` topic of `public/default`, those created after startup included. b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::pattern("persistent://public/default/orders-.*", "audit"), Audit, ) .build(), ); }, ) }

PulsarSubscription::new joins a named durable subscription on one topic: a bare name, tenant/namespace/topic, or a full name. The first argument is the topic, and the second is the subscription. A bare name is a topic of persistent://public/default, a triple is a persistent topic of that tenant and namespace, and a full name such as non-persistent://acme/sales/pings says everything itself. The subscription is the cursor the server keeps for its readers. Every consumer that joins the same subscription shares one backlog, and a second subscription on the same topic reads every message again, from a cursor of its own. subscription() returns the name. Every setting has a default, so the two names are all a descriptor needs: Setting What it does Default subscription_type how the consumers of the subscription share it Shared ack_timeout redelivers what a handler left unsettled longer than this none batch_wait how long a batch that is not full waits for more deliveries 10 ms The subscription reports under its topic, as written: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and the AsyncAPI document reports that channel. A topic name Pulsar would refuse stops the service at startup with an error that names it, before any call to the server; PulsarTopic is the same check as a type. Topics and subscriptions reads one topic under two subscriptions of a fulfilment service.

Billing and shipping read every order of acme/sales/orders, each under a subscription of its own. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// Bills every order of the `acme/sales` namespace; the subscription `billing` is its cursor. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("acme/sales/orders", "billing"))] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Ships the same orders on a cursor of its own. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("acme/sales/orders", "shipping"))] async fn ship(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(bill); b.include(ship); }) } examples/manual/pulsar_subscriptions_descriptor.rs /// Bills every order of the `acme/sales` namespace. struct Bill; impl Handle<Order> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Ships the same orders. struct Ship; impl Handle<Order> for Ship { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Each subscription is a cursor of its own: `billing` and `shipping` read every order. b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("acme/sales/orders", "billing"), Bill, ) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("acme/sales/orders", "shipping"), Ship, ) .build(), ); }) }

PulsarTopic is a topic name checked on construction: persistent and non_persistent for literals, parse for names read at run time. A Pulsar topic name carries four things: the persistence, the tenant, the namespace and the topic. Each of the last three may hold ASCII letters, digits, -, _ and ., and none may be empty. PulsarTopic::persistent and PulsarTopic::non_persistent build a name from its parts and panic on a part Pulsar would refuse, so they are for names written in the code. PulsarTopic::parse is the form for a name that arrives at run time. It accepts a full name, a tenant/namespace/topic triple, which is persistent, or a bare name, which belongs to persistent://public/default, and returns an error for anything else. as_str is the full name, and Display writes the same. persistence, tenant, namespace and name return the parts. A descriptor and a publish parse every topic they are given the same way, so a name Pulsar would refuse never reaches the server: a descriptor stops the service at startup, and a publish returns an error. Topics and subscriptions names the topics of a fulfilment service.

Each order goes to its tenant's own topic; an order naming a tenant that is no valid name part is dropped. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_subscriptions_topic.rs /// The tenants' own order topics. #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Order)] struct TenantOrders; /// Fans orders out to their tenant's topic. The tenant comes off the wire, so its topic is /// parsed, and an order naming a tenant Pulsar would refuse is dropped here. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "router"))] async fn route(order: &Order, Out(tenants): Out<impl Publisher, TenantOrders>) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(topic) = PulsarTopic::parse(&format!("{}/orders/created", order.tenant)) else { tracing::warn!(order.id, tenant = %order.tenant, "no such tenant topic"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; match tenants.message(order).to(topic.as_str()).publish().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("router", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(route).out(TenantOrders, Publish).build(); }) } examples/manual/pulsar_subscriptions_topic.rs /// The tenants' own order topics. struct TenantOrders; impl OutSlot for TenantOrders { const NAME: &'static str = "TenantOrders"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<TenantOrders> for Order {} /// Fans orders out to their tenant's topic. The tenant comes off the wire, so its topic is /// parsed, and an order naming a tenant Pulsar would refuse is dropped here. struct Route; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Route where Entry: OutEntry<TenantOrders, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ok(topic) = PulsarTopic::parse(&format!("{}/orders/created", order.tenant)) else { tracing::warn!(order.id, tenant = %order.tenant, "no such tenant topic"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); }; let tenants = outs.get(TenantOrders); match tenants.message(order).to(topic.as_str()).publish().await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), Err(_) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), } } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("router", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "router"), Route).build()) .out(TenantOrders, Publish) .build(); }) }

SubscriptionType says how the consumers of one subscription share it: Exclusive, Shared, Failover or KeyShared. PulsarSubscription::subscription_type sets it, and Shared is the default. Each handler mounted on a subscription is one consumer of it, and so is each instance of the service. A message reaches every subscription on its topic once, and the type decides which consumer of the subscription takes it: Type Who takes a message Exclusive the one consumer of the subscription; a second consumer waits until the first leaves Shared any consumer, in turn Failover the active consumer; a standby takes over when it leaves KeyShared the consumer that holds the message's key, so one key is read in order The server refuses a second Exclusive consumer as busy, and the client asks again until its operation retries run out; with the default retries it asks for ever, so the second instance does not finish starting. An Exclusive subscription belongs to a service that runs one instance. Under the test harness that second consumer is refused at startup instead, so the test fails rather than hangs. A message's key is its partition key. A retry cap needs Shared or KeyShared, because only there does the server count a message's redeliveries; a cap on the other two stops the service at startup, as Dead letters explains. Subscription types and ordering reads a shipping service under each of the four types.

Two workers on the Shared subscription workers: each task runs once, on one of them. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_subscriptions_type.rs /// Two workers attach to the subscription `workers`: each task goes to one of them. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("tasks", "workers").subscription_type(SubscriptionType::Shared) )] async fn first_worker(task: &Task) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(task.id, "first worker ran the task"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("tasks", "workers").subscription_type(SubscriptionType::Shared) )] async fn second_worker(task: &Task) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(task.id, "second worker ran the task"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("workers", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(first_worker); b.include(second_worker); }) } examples/manual/pulsar_subscriptions_type.rs /// One worker; the service runs two of them on one subscription. struct Worker(&'static str); impl Handle<Task> for Worker { fn handle( &self, task: &Task, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(task.id, worker = self.0, "task ran"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("workers", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Both workers attach to the subscription `workers`: each task goes to one of them. for name in ["first", "second"] { b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("tasks", "workers") .subscription_type(SubscriptionType::Shared), Worker(name), ) .build(), ); } }) }

PulsarSubscription::topics reads a fixed list of topics under one subscription; one seek or one retry policy covers them all. The first argument is the list, and each topic in it takes any of the three spellings a single topic takes. The subscription keeps a cursor on every topic of the list, and its consumers read all of them. A list has no single topic to name the subscription by, so it reports under the subscription's own name: a test reads its deliveries under that name, and the AsyncAPI document reports that channel. A seek from a handler moves the cursor on every topic of the list. The registration's dead-letter topic is one for the whole list. The settings and their defaults are those of PulsarSubscription. An empty list, or a name in it that Pulsar would refuse, stops the service at startup. Topics and subscriptions totals the orders of two regional topics under one subscription.

The European and the American orders, fulfilled under one subscription. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_subscriptions_topics.rs /// Reads the European and the American orders under one subscription, `regional`. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::topics(["orders-eu", "orders-us"], "regional"))] async fn fulfil(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, region = %order.region, "order fulfilled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("fulfilment", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(fulfil); }) } examples/manual/pulsar_subscriptions_topics.rs /// Fulfils the European and the American orders. struct Fulfil; impl Handle<Order> for Fulfil { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, region = %order.region, "order fulfilled"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("fulfilment", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Two topics under one subscription, `regional`, which is also its reported name. b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::topics(["orders-eu", "orders-us"], "regional"), Fulfil, ) .build(), ); }) }

TestApp::start connects PulsarBroker in process: topics, the four subscription types, dead letters, delayed retries and seeking. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The in-process mode has no settings of its own. The default subscription, each descriptor's settings, the retry cap and its dead-letter topic, and the payload limit are the broker's and the registration's. So a test runs the configuration production runs. It refuses what a server refuses, with the same error: a service URL the client cannot parse, a destination that is no topic name, a payload over the limit, and a handle used after shutdown. A second consumer of an Exclusive subscription is refused at once, where a server would keep it waiting. The mode keeps Pulsar's semantics: orders and persistent://public/default/orders are one topic. A message reaches every subscription over its topic once, and the subscription type picks the consumer within one. A negatively acknowledged delivery goes back to its subscription, and the dead-letter policy counts deliveries as the client does. A subscription starts at the end of its topics, and a seek moves it over the log the test published. A pattern reads a topic created later from the next listing, thirty seconds on. A header value that is not UTF-8 text fails the publish, as the client frames headers as text. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply and a dead-letter move included. The assertions that follow read finished state. A delayed retry and a pattern's listing run on the runtime's clock, so tb.advance on a paused clock drives both. What only a server has is for a live test. Testing a Pulsar service tests a card payments service in process.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-pulsar = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } The first test publishes an empty payment and reads how the handler settled it. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_empty_payment_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 0 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called_once() .with(&Payment { amount: 0 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); Ok(()) } examples/manual/pulsar_testing.rs #[tokio::test] async fn an_empty_payment_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 0 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called_once() .with(&Payment { amount: 0 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); Ok(()) } A payment over the review limit is retried after a minute. On a paused clock the minute passes when the test advances it. Macros Manual examples/pulsar_testing.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_held_payment_is_read_again_after_the_review_delay() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 50_000 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(REVIEW)); // The clock is paused: the delay passes when the test says so, not in real time. tb.advance(REVIEW).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called(2); Ok(()) } examples/manual/pulsar_testing.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_held_payment_is_read_again_after_the_review_delay() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 50_000 }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(REVIEW)); // The clock is paused: the delay passes when the test says so, not in real time. tb.advance(REVIEW).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("payments") .assert_called(2); Ok(()) }

TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running Pulsar, for what only a server has. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so the client dials the server and every subscription opens a real consumer. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process mode leaves to the server: the ack timeout's own redelivery; partitioned topics, and the partition a key picks; which consumer of a Shared or KeyShared subscription the server picks, and KeyShared hash ranges; messages published while a subscription has no consumer; a second Exclusive consumer waiting, and the OperationRetries that bound the wait; the token and TLS; a backlog older than the test, which start_at replays. A server keeps what earlier runs left in it, and a subscription is a durable cursor on it. So each run reads in a subscription of its own, which starts at the end of the topic, past what earlier runs published. In the example, stand returns the server's URL from PULSAR_TEST_URL, and the live test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no server. A job that stood a server up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing URL then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, a Pulsar standalone on 127.0.0.1:6650 that just brokers-up starts. Testing a Pulsar service runs the same test against a server.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the server at PULSAR_TEST_URL. tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("testing-live-payments") .assert_called_once() .with(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { accepts_a_payment(TestApp::start(app("pulsar://localhost:6650", "payments-svc")).await?) .await } #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn against_the_stand() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = stand() else { return Ok(()); }; // A subscription of this run's own: it starts at the end of the topic, past what // earlier runs published, and its cursor outlives the test on the server. let subscription = format!("payments-{}", process::id()); accepts_a_payment(TestApp::start_live(app(&url, &subscription)).await?).await } examples/manual/pulsar_testing_live.rs /// The body both modes run; only the start call differs. async fn accepts_a_payment(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&Payment { amount: 100 }) .publish() .await?; This guide settles Pulsar messages by the handler's outcome, bounds an unsettled delivery with an acknowledgement timeout, and settles a batch at once. The example is an inventory service. It reserves stock for orders and records the stock counts of warehouse scans. Stock stands in for the client of the stock service, and the app opens it at startup.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Reservation { order: u64, sku: String, quantity: u32, } /// Reserves stock for an order. A reservation left unsettled for a minute comes back. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("reservations", "inventory").ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(60)) )] async fn reserve(reservation: &Reservation, State(stock): State<Arc<Stock>>) -> HandlerOutcome { match stock.reserve(reservation).await { Ok(()) => { tracing::info!(reservation.order, reservation.quantity, "stock reserved"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } // No answer: the subscription hands the reservation out again at once. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Err(Refusal::UnknownSku) => { tracing::warn!(reservation.order, "unknown SKU, reservation dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Reservation { order: u64, sku: String, quantity: u32, } /// A reservation left unsettled for a minute comes back. fn reservations() -> PulsarSubscription { PulsarSubscription::new("reservations", "inventory").ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(60)) } /// Reserves stock for an order. struct Reserve; impl Handle<Reservation, (), (), (), Clients> for Reserve { async fn handle( &self, reservation: &Reservation, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match ctx.state().stock.reserve(reservation).await { Ok(()) => { tracing::info!(reservation.order, reservation.quantity, "stock reserved"); Ok(()) } // No answer: the subscription hands the reservation out again at once. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), Err(Refusal::UnknownSku) => { tracing::warn!(reservation.order, "unknown SKU, reservation dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } } The value reserve returns decides what happens to the message on Pulsar: Outcome On Pulsar ack the message is acknowledged and never comes back retry the message is negatively acknowledged and delivered again at once retry_after(delay) the message is held for delay, then negatively acknowledged drop the message is acknowledged A stock service that does not answer may answer the next call, so reserve retries. The message goes back to the subscription, and on a Shared subscription another consumer may take it. A SKU that no item carries stays unknown, so reserve drops the reservation. Pulsar has no verb to reject a message for good, so drop acknowledges it, and the message is gone. A message that keeps failing leaves the subscription through a dead-letter topic instead. The client sends acknowledgements in the background. A settlement that returns is queued on the consumer, and the broker records it a moment later. A service that stops in between gets the message again on its next start, so Pulsar delivers each message at least once. Handle a message so that a second delivery does no harm, for example by keying the work on the order's id.

A delivery that nobody settles stays with its consumer. ack_timeout on the descriptor gives it a limit: the client asks the broker to deliver the message again once the limit has passed. Without it, such a message comes back only when its consumer disconnects. Set the timeout above the longest time the handler takes. A handler still at work when the timeout passes gets a second delivery of the same message. Each redelivery counts toward the retry cap, like a retry.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Count { sku: String, on_hand: u32, } /// Records the stock counts of a warehouse scan, many counts per call. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("stock-counts", "inventory").batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(250)) )] async fn record_counts(counts: &[Count], State(stock): State<Arc<Stock>>) -> HandlerOutcome { stock.record(counts).await; tracing::info!(counts = counts.len(), "stock counts recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Count { sku: String, on_hand: u32, } /// A batch that is not full closes 250 ms after its first count. fn stock_counts() -> PulsarSubscription { PulsarSubscription::new("stock-counts", "inventory").batch_wait(Duration::from_millis(250)) } /// Records the stock counts of a warehouse scan; `Ok` settles the whole batch. struct RecordCounts; impl Handle<[Count], (), (), (), Clients> for RecordCounts { async fn handle( &self, counts: &[Count], _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>> { ctx.state().stock.record(counts).await; tracing::info!(counts = counts.len(), "stock counts recorded"); Ok(()) } } A handler over a slice is a batch handler. The Pulsar client hands over one message at a time, so the service assembles the batch. A batch closes when it is full or when batch_wait has passed since its first message, here 250 milliseconds. One outcome settles every message of the batch. In the manual form, Ok(()) acknowledges the batch, and Err(outcomes) settles each message with its own outcome.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inventory", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(reserve); b.include(record_counts.batch(nonzero!(64))); }) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("inventory", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(reservations(), Reserve).build()); b.include( subscriber(stock_counts(), RecordCounts) .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build(), ); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } batch(n) at the mount site is the largest batch, 64 counts here. on_startup opens the clients once, and the handlers read them as the app's state.

The tests in the example file run the app in process, with TestApp::with_state in place of on_startup. They make the stock service fail on purpose and check the outcome of each delivery. The in-process Pulsar hands a negatively acknowledged message back to the subscription, as a server does. The redelivery after the acknowledgement timeout is the server's, and the crate's live tests check it against a running Pulsar.
This guide installs ruststream-pulsar, starts a local Pulsar and runs a first service against it.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.7", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-pulsar = "0.7" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-pulsar = { version = "0.7", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-pulsar is the Pulsar broker. Its testing feature adds the in-process Pulsar that tests run on. The broker crate has these features, both off by default: Feature What it gives testing the in-process Pulsar behind TestApp asyncapi the Pulsar bindings in the generated AsyncAPI document

The Pulsar client compiles the Pulsar protocol definitions during the build, so the build needs protoc, the Protocol Buffers compiler. On Debian and Ubuntu it comes with protobuf-compiler, and on macOS with brew install protobuf. A protoc outside the path is named by the PROTOC environment variable.

Pulsar in standalone mode runs a broker and its storage in one container: compose.yaml services: pulsar: image: apachepulsar/pulsar:4.1.2 command: bin/pulsar standalone ports: - "6650:6650" - "8080:8080" environment: # The address the broker hands to clients outside the container. PULSAR_PREFIX_advertisedAddress: 127.0.0.1 PULSAR_PREFIX_advertisedListeners: pulsar://127.0.0.1:6650 healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/admin/v2/brokers/health || exit 1"] interval: 10s retries: 30 Start it and wait until it is healthy: docker compose up -d --wait The broker listens on localhost:6650, and the admin API on localhost:8080. Pulsar creates a topic on its first use, so the service needs no setup.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "billing"))] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(take_order); }, ) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "billing"), TakeOrder).build()); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order reads JSON orders from the orders topic. It acknowledges an order with an amount and drops one without. Pulsar reads a topic only through a named subscription. PulsarSubscription::new names the topic and the subscription, here billing. The subscription is a cursor the server keeps, so the service resumes where it stopped after a restart. PulsarBroker::new takes the service URL and only records it. The connection opens when the service starts. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run Publish an order from another terminal with the client that ships in the image: docker compose exec pulsar bin/pulsar-client produce orders \ -s ';' -m '{"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' -s ';' keeps the message whole: by default the client splits it at every comma. The service logs order taken with the order's id. Ctrl+C stops it.

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes an order and checks how take_order settled it. PulsarBroker connects to an in-process Pulsar there, so the tests need no server: cargo test Testing a Pulsar service walks through these tests and what the in-process Pulsar models.

A service on the pulsar crate builds its own client, consumer loop and producers. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: pulsar crate RustStream Pulsar::builder(url, TokioExecutor).build().await PulsarBroker::new(url), connected by the runtime .with_auth(Authentication { name: "token", .. }) PulsarBroker::token .with_operation_retry_options(..) PulsarBroker::operation_retries client.consumer().with_topic(..).with_subscription(..) and a loop over the consumer a #[subscriber] handler on a PulsarSubscription .with_subscription_type(..) subscription_type on the descriptor .with_topics([..]), .with_topic_regex(..) PulsarSubscription::topics, PulsarSubscription::pattern deserializing msg.payload.data the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec consumer.ack(&msg), consumer.nack(&msg) the handler's outcome (Acknowledgement) .with_dead_letter_policy(..) max_attempts(n) and dead_letter(topic) at the mount site (Retries and dead letters) .with_unacked_message_resend_delay(..) ack_timeout on the descriptor consumer.seek(..) start_at at the mount site, or the seek handle in the handler (Replay and seeking) client.producer().with_topic(..).build() and send_non_blocking a reply or an Out parameter, sent through the publish policy (Publishing and replies) producer::Message { partition_key, properties, .. } the partition_key step; headers become properties
A production cluster asks for TLS and authentication, and a service decides how long it waits for the cluster and how large a message it sends.

src/main.rs /// Where the cluster is and who the service is, as the deployment provides them. struct Cluster { url: String, token: String, } impl Cluster { fn from_env() -> Self { let read = |name: &str| env::var(name).unwrap_or_default(); Self { url: read("PULSAR_URL"), token: read("PULSAR_TOKEN"), } } } fn broker(cluster: Cluster) -> PulsarBroker { // Ten tries, three seconds apart; then the error. let retries = OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(10u32)).delay(Duration::from_secs(3)); PulsarBroker::new(cluster.url) .token(cluster.token) .operation_retries(retries) // The cluster runs with `maxMessageSize=10485760`. .max_message_size(nonzero!(10_485_760usize)) } The deployment provides the service URL and the token in environment variables. A Pulsar client dials one service URL. A cluster of several brokers is reached through one entry point in front of them: a DNS name, a load balancer or the Pulsar proxy. A pulsar+ssl:// URL dials the cluster's TLS listener, port 6651 by convention. The client checks the server's certificate against the system's trusted roots, and its host name. token authenticates with a JWT, which the client sends when it connects and when it reconnects. StreamNative Cloud and a self-hosted cluster with token authentication both take this pair.

The client reconnects on its own after a broker restart, and asks again for any operation the cluster has not accepted yet. By default it asks for ever, five seconds apart, which waits out a restart of any length. OperationRetries bounds that: ten tries three seconds apart, and then the operation fails with the cluster's answer. The bound covers the lookups, the producers and the reconnect of every consumer. It also turns a second consumer of an Exclusive subscription into an error at startup instead of a wait. max_message_size is the largest payload a publish may carry, five mebibytes by default as on the server. A deployment that changed the server's maxMessageSize sets the same value here. A larger publish fails in the service, before it reaches the cluster.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "orders-svc"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { id: order.id } } fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(confirm); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service(broker(Cluster::from_env())) } src/main.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "orders-svc"), Confirm) .reply() .build(), ); }) } fn app() -> RustStream { service(broker(Cluster::from_env())) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } Every setting of the broker is a builder step that dials nothing, so #[ruststream::app] builds the app as it does locally. The connection opens when the service starts. The generated AsyncAPI document reports the host and the port of the URL, and never the token. A service that replays its topics also needs the namespace's retention policy on the cluster.

The tests start the production service with the production broker, given a test token, under TestApp::start. The in-process Pulsar checks the service URL as the client parses it, without dialling the cluster. A URL with another scheme fails the start, and the error names the schemes the client dials: the service URL's scheme "https" is not one the client dials: pulsar or pulsar+ssl TLS, the token and the retry bound take effect only on a real cluster.

This guide replies to Pulsar messages, publishes keyed messages with headers through an Out slot, and publishes once the service has started. The example is a checkout service. It confirms orders with receipts, answers price quotes, sends pick lists to warehouses and announces itself at startup.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The receipt of an order; the type names the topic it goes to. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } /// Confirms each order with a receipt. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "receipts"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Receipt { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Receipt { order: order.id } } src/main.rs /// The receipt of an order; the type names the topic it goes to. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order: u64, } /// Confirms each order with a receipt. struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Receipt { order: order.id })) } } confirm returns a Receipt, and the framework publishes it. #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] fixes the topic on the type, so the subscriber writes the bare reply clause; in the manual form, .reply(). The broker's publish policy, Publish in the prelude, is its default, so a plain include replies through it. A publish returns once the broker has stored the message.
documents.s: A reply to a declared topic

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct QuoteRequest { request: u64, items: u32, } /// A price quote; the mount site names where it goes. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Quote { request: u64, total_cents: u64, } /// Answers a quote request on `quotes`, the topic the requesting services read. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("quote-requests", "quotes"), reply("quotes"))] async fn quote(request: &QuoteRequest) -> Quote { Quote { request: request.request, total_cents: u64::from(request.items) * 1_250, } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct QuoteRequest { request: u64, items: u32, } /// A price quote; the mount site names where it goes. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] struct Quote { request: u64, total_cents: u64, } /// Answers a quote request on `quotes`, the topic the requesting services read. struct AnswerQuote; impl Handle<QuoteRequest, Quote> for AnswerQuote { fn handle( &self, request: &QuoteRequest, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Quote, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Quote { request: request.request, total_cents: u64::from(request.items) * 1_250, })) } } Quote names no topic, so reply("quotes") names it at the mount site; in the manual form, .reply().to("quotes"). The same type can then answer on another topic in another service. A request and its answer travel on two ordinary topics. A service that asks for quotes publishes to quote-requests and reads quotes under a subscription of its own. It matches each quote to its request by the request id the two messages share.
documents.s: A reply to a topic the mount site names

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs /// A pick list for the warehouse that ships the order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "warehouse-picks")] struct Pick { order: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Pick)] struct Picks; /// Sends each order to its warehouse, keyed by the warehouse so its picks stay in order. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "dispatch"))] async fn dispatch( order: &Order, Out(picks): Out<impl Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>, Picks>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("source", "checkout"); let sent = picks .message(&Pick { order: order.id }) .with_headers(headers) .partition_key(order.warehouse.clone()) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(error) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, %error, "pick list not sent"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } src/main.rs /// A pick list for the warehouse that ships the order. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "warehouse-picks")] struct Pick { order: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Pick)] struct Picks; /// Sends each order to its warehouse, keyed by the warehouse so its picks stay in order. struct Dispatch; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Dispatch where Entry: OutEntry<Picks, Wire: Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("source", "checkout"); outs.get(Picks) .message(&Pick { order: order.id }) .with_headers(headers) .partition_key(order.warehouse.clone()) .publish() .await .map_err(|error| { tracing::warn!(order.id, %error, "pick list not sent"); HandlerOutcome::retry() }) } } An Out slot publishes from the handler's body, and Picks declares the type it carries. partition_key keys each pick list by its warehouse. On a partitioned topic the key picks the partition, and a KeyShared subscription keeps the order of each key. The step comes from the broker's prelude, so the slot is bounded Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions> to offer it. Each header becomes a message property of the same name. A consumer in another language reads source as an ordinary Pulsar property, with no envelope around the payload. Pulsar carries properties as text, so a header value that is not UTF-8 fails the publish. A publish that fails returns the error, and dispatch retries the order. A payload larger than the broker's max_message_size, five mebibytes by default, fails before it is sent.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Tells the rest of the system that checkout is up. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "service-events")] struct Started { service: String, } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include(confirm); b.include(quote); b.include(dispatch).out(Picks, Publish).build(); b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "checkout".to_owned(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }, ) } src/main.rs /// Tells the rest of the system that checkout is up. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "service-events")] struct Started { service: String, } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("checkout", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "receipts"), Confirm) .reply() .build(), ); b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("quote-requests", "quotes"), AnswerQuote, ) .reply() .to("quotes") .build(), ); b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "dispatch"), Dispatch).build()) .out(Picks, Publish) .build(); b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { let started = Started { service: "checkout".to_owned(), }; publisher.message(&started).publish().await }); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } .out(Picks, Publish) wires the slot to the publish policy. after_startup runs once the subscriptions are open, with a publisher of the policy it names, and checkout announces itself on service-events. A hook that fails stops the service at startup. The publisher opens one producer per topic on the first publish to it, and shutdown closes them. Code outside the app takes a publisher from the broker: PulsarBroker::publisher before the service starts, and ConnectedPulsarBroker::publisher after.

The tests in the example file run the app in process. published checks what reached a topic, with its headers, and tb.out::<Picks>() checks the key the slot's publish carried. The in-process Pulsar frames headers and the key the way the client does, so a header the server would refuse fails the test too.

This guide reads a Pulsar topic's retained log again: from the start on every startup, or from a position a handler seeks to. A subscription is a cursor on the topic's log, and the server keeps it. A seek moves that cursor, and the subscription reads on from its new place. The example is a search service. It keeps account balances built from a ledger, and a search index of orders. Search stands in for the client of the search cluster.

PulsarPosition names a place in a topic's log: Position Where PulsarPosition::earliest() the oldest retained message PulsarPosition::latest() the end of the log: only messages published after the seek PulsarPosition::timestamp(millis) the first message published at or after that time, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch PulsarPosition::MessageId(..) a delivered message, read from its Position

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Rebuilds the account balances from the oldest retained entry on every startup. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("ledger", "balances"), start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()) )] async fn project(entry: &Entry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.account, entry.amount_cents, "balance updated"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Rebuilds the account balances; the mount site starts it at the oldest retained entry. struct Project; impl Handle<Entry, (), (), (), Clients> for Project { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.account, entry.amount_cents, "balance updated"); ready(Ok(())) } } start_at seeks the subscription each time the service starts. balances reads the ledger from its oldest retained entry on every start, so the balances are rebuilt from scratch. Without start_at, an existing subscription resumes where its consumers stopped, and a new one starts at the end of the topic. Pulsar has an initial position of its own, but it applies only when a subscription is created. start_at applies to the subscription that already exists too. Every instance that starts moves the shared cursor, so the instances of a service with start_at replay the log at each start of any of them.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, } /// Indexes each order; a lost index sends the subscription back to the oldest retained order. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "search-index"))] async fn index( order: &Order, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>, State(search): State<Arc<Search>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { match search.index(order).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(SearchError::IndexLost) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, "index lost, indexing every order again"); if seeker.seek(PulsarPosition::earliest()).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, } /// Indexes each order; a lost index sends the subscription back to the oldest retained order. struct Index; impl Handle<Order, (), (), PulsarContext, Clients> for Index { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PulsarContext, Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match ctx.state().search.index(order).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), Err(SearchError::IndexLost) => { tracing::warn!(order.id, "index lost, indexing every order again"); ctx.context(SeekHandle) .seek(PulsarPosition::earliest()) .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } } } SeekHandle is the subscription's own seeker, and index reads it from the Pulsar context. When the search cluster loses its index, index seeks to the oldest retained order, and every order is indexed again. In the manual form the handler names PulsarContext as its context and reads the seeker with ctx.context(SeekHandle). A seek moves the whole subscription: every consumer of it, every topic it reads and every partition. Deliveries already queued for the subscription are discarded, and the log is read from the new place. Two other seeks come up often: PulsarPosition::timestamp(millis) skips a stretch of bad data: the subscription resumes at the first message published after it. A delivery's position, read with Ctx<Position>, delivers exactly that message again, then the rest of the log in order. A batch handler seeks the same way through PulsarBatchContext, which carries the seeker and no position, because a batch spans many messages.

A replay reads what the topic still holds. By default Pulsar deletes a message once every subscription has acknowledged it. A retention policy on the namespace keeps acknowledged messages for a size or a time: docker compose exec pulsar bin/pulsar-admin namespaces set-retention public/default \ --size 1G --time 3d A non-persistent topic keeps nothing, so a seek there replays nothing.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("search", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(project); b.include(index); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650")) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: PulsarBroker) -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("search", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("ledger", "balances"), Project) .start_at(PulsarPosition::earliest()) .build(), ); b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "search-index"), Index).build()); }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { service(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650")) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } service builds the app on the broker it is given, so a test can take a publisher off that broker before the app starts.

The tests in the example file run the app in process. The in-process Pulsar keeps each topic's log, so a seek there replays it as a server does. The test publishes three orders in one burst through broker.publisher(), so all three wait in the subscription before the first one is handled. tb.settle() then waits until the subscription is idle. A backlog left by an earlier run of the service exists only on a server, so start_at over such a backlog is checked by the crate's live tests.

This guide retries a Pulsar message now or later, caps the deliveries, and moves what keeps failing to a dead-letter topic that a handler reads. Pulsar redelivers a message itself, so a retry publishes nothing. The mount site declares the cap and the dead-letter topic, and the Pulsar client applies them. The example is a refunds service that sends refunds through a card processor. Processor stands in for the processor's client, and the app opens it at startup.

The processor refuses a refund in three ways, and each needs a different outcome. Busy means its rate limit is used up: a retry right now would be refused again, so retry_after waits 30 seconds. Unavailable means it did not answer: retry tries again at once. Declined means the card account is closed, and another try gets the same answer, so the refund is dropped. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "refunds")] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } /// A refund left unsettled for two minutes comes back; a wait must be shorter than that. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("refunds", "refunds").ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(120)))] async fn process_refund( refund: &Refund, State(processor): State<Arc<Processor>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { match processor.refund(refund).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "refunds")] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } /// A refund left unsettled for two minutes comes back; a wait must be shorter than that. fn refunds() -> PulsarSubscription { PulsarSubscription::new("refunds", "refunds").ack_timeout(Duration::from_secs(120)) } struct ProcessRefund; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for ProcessRefund { async fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match ctx.state().processor.refund(refund).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } } retry negatively acknowledges the refund, and the broker delivers it again at once. retry_after holds the refund unacknowledged in the service for the delay, then negatively acknowledges it. Pulsar's negative acknowledgement carries no delay of its own, so the wait belongs to the process. A process that stops during the wait loses the wait, not the refund: the broker delivers it again after the acknowledgement timeout, or at once when the consumer disconnects. The delay has to be shorter than the subscription's acknowledgement timeout, or the timeout would bring the refund back first. A longer delay is refused when the handler returns it, with an error that names both values. A subscription without an acknowledgement timeout accepts any delay.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter topic. b.include(process_refund) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds-dlq"); b.include(review); }) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter topic. b.include(subscriber(refunds(), ProcessRefund).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds-dlq"); b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("refunds-dlq", "refunds-review"), Review, ) .build(), ); }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts counts every delivery of one refund, the first included. dead_letter names where a refund goes once the deliveries are spent. The pair becomes the consumer's own dead-letter policy. The Pulsar client counts the redeliveries, publishes the fifth failed refund to refunds-dlq and acknowledges the original. A retry, a retry_after and an expired acknowledgement timeout each count as a redelivery. A dropped refund settles and goes nowhere; the dead-letter topic holds only the refunds that ran out of attempts. Write both steps or neither: a cap without a destination, or a destination without a cap, stops the service at startup, and the error names the missing step. The broker counts redeliveries only on a Shared or a KeyShared subscription, so the cap belongs there. A cap on an Exclusive or a Failover subscription would never be reached, and such a registration stops the service at startup with an error that names the type. A handler mounted by a bare topic name takes the same declaration, on the broker's default subscription.

documents.t: The dead-letter topic is an ordinary topic, and review reads it like any other. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Reads the refunds that ran out of attempts. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("refunds-dlq", "refunds-review"))] async fn review(refund: &Refund) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(refund.id, "refund needs a person to look at it"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Reads the refunds that ran out of attempts. struct Review; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for Review { fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::error!(refund.id, "refund needs a person to look at it"); ready(Ok(())) } } A dead-lettered refund keeps the payload and the headers it arrived with. The client adds two properties: REAL_TOPIC, the topic the refund came from, and ORIGIN_MESSAGE_ID, its position there. review logs the refund for a person to look at.

The tests in the example file run the app in process with TestApp::with_state, which hands the handlers a processor that fails on purpose. The delay test starts on a paused clock, so tb.advance(BACKOFF) lets the 30 seconds pass at once. The in-process Pulsar counts the deliveries and moves the spent refund to refunds-dlq the way the client does. Testing a Pulsar service covers the harness.

This guide chooses how the consumers of a Pulsar subscription share it, keeps the order of each key, and places keyed messages on partitions. The example is a shipping service. It packs orders, tracks shipments, books payments and invoices orders, and each of these reads under a different subscription type.

Every consumer of a subscription is a handler in one of the service's instances. The subscription type decides how those consumers share the messages: Type Who gets a message Order Shared (default) any consumer, in turn none KeyShared the consumer that holds the message's key per key Exclusive the one consumer; a second one waits for it the topic's order Failover the active consumer; the others stand by the topic's order subscription_type on the descriptor sets the type. Every consumer of one subscription names the same type.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// One step in the life of a shipment. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments")] struct Shipment { order: u64, status: String, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; /// Packs an order. Every instance of the service shares the subscription `packing`. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "packing"))] async fn pack( order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>, Shipments>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let packed = Shipment { order: order.id, status: "packed".to_owned(), }; // The order's id keys the event, so every event of one order keeps its place in line. let sent = shipments .message(&packed) .partition_key(order.id.to_string()) .publish() .await; if sent.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, "order packed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// One step in the life of a shipment. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments")] struct Shipment { order: u64, status: String, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Shipment)] struct Shipments; /// Packs an order. Every instance of the service shares the subscription `packing`. struct Pack; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Pack where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let packed = Shipment { order: order.id, status: "packed".to_owned(), }; // The order's id keys the event, so every event of one order keeps its place in line. outs.get(Shipments) .message(&packed) .partition_key(order.id.to_string()) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; tracing::info!(order.id, "order packed"); Ok(()) } } Shared hands each order to one consumer of packing, whichever is next. More instances of the service pack more orders at once, and two orders may finish in any order. That suits work whose messages do not depend on each other. pack publishes a shipment event for each order. The partition_key step keys the event by the order's id. The step comes from the broker's prelude, so the slot is bounded Publisher<Options = PulsarPublishOptions> to offer it. A publish returns once the broker has stored the message.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Follows each shipment. Events of one order arrive in the order they were published. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("shipments", "tracking") .subscription_type(SubscriptionType::KeyShared), workers(8, by_key) )] async fn track(event: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.order, event.status, "shipment tracked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Follows each shipment. Events of one order arrive in the order they were published. struct Track; impl Handle<Shipment> for Track { fn handle( &self, event: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.order, event.status, "shipment tracked"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn tracking() -> PulsarSubscription { PulsarSubscription::new("shipments", "tracking").subscription_type(SubscriptionType::KeyShared) } KeyShared gives all the messages of one key to one consumer, so the events of one order reach track in the order pack published them. Different keys spread over the consumers, so the instances share the work. The server assigns the keys and moves some of them when a consumer joins or leaves. Inside one instance, workers(8, by_key) runs eight lanes, and the deliveries of one key run one after another on one lane. The lane key is the message's partition key, so the order of each key holds within the process too. In the manual form the same setting is workers_by_key. The key reaches the handler as the partition-key header.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Books payments one after another, in the order they were taken. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("payments", "ledger").subscription_type(SubscriptionType::Exclusive) )] async fn book(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(payment.order, payment.amount_cents, "payment booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Books payments one after another, in the order they were taken. struct Book; impl Handle<Payment> for Book { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(payment.order, payment.amount_cents, "payment booked"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn ledger() -> PulsarSubscription { PulsarSubscription::new("payments", "ledger").subscription_type(SubscriptionType::Exclusive) } Exclusive lets one consumer read the subscription, so book sees the payments in the order they were taken. The server refuses a second consumer as busy, and the client keeps asking until the first one leaves or OperationRetries runs out, which by default is never. So a second instance of the service does not start, and reports nothing while it waits. An Exclusive subscription belongs to a service that runs one instance.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Invoices orders on one instance at a time; the others stand by. #[subscriber( PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "invoicing").subscription_type(SubscriptionType::Failover) )] async fn invoice(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order invoiced"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Invoices orders on one instance at a time; the others stand by. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order> for Invoice { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order invoiced"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn invoicing() -> PulsarSubscription { PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "invoicing").subscription_type(SubscriptionType::Failover) } Failover accepts every consumer but delivers to one of them. The others are hot standbys: when the active one disconnects, the server hands its messages to the next. Several instances keep the order of an Exclusive subscription without its single point of failure. On a partitioned topic each partition has its own active consumer, so the instances share the partitions.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // A second ledger consumer reports the refusal after three tries instead of waiting. let retries = OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(3u32)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").operation_retries(retries), |b| { b.include(pack).out(Shipments, Publish).build(); b.include(track); b.include(book); b.include(invoice); }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { // A second ledger consumer reports the refusal after three tries instead of waiting. let retries = OperationRetries::attempts(nonzero!(3u32)); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").operation_retries(retries), |b| { b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "packing"), Pack).build()) .out(Shipments, Publish) .build(); b.include( subscriber(tracking(), Track) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8usize)) .build(), ); b.include(subscriber(ledger(), Book).build()); b.include(subscriber(invoicing(), Invoice).build()); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } OperationRetries::attempts bounds how often the client asks again for an operation the server has not accepted. With three attempts, a second consumer of ledger stops the service at startup with an error that names the topic. The bound covers every operation of the connection, the reconnect after a broker restart included, so it trades waiting out an outage for an early error.

A partitioned topic is several topics under one name, and each partition is served on its own. An administrator creates it with its number of partitions: docker compose exec pulsar bin/pulsar-admin topics create-partitioned-topic \ persistent://public/default/shipments -p 3 A subscription reads every partition of the topic, and a service reads it with the same descriptor as any other topic. A keyed message goes to the partition its key hashes to, so the messages of one key stay in one partition and in order. Unkeyed messages go to the partitions in turn.

The tests in the example file run the app in process. There, each subscription gets every message of its topic once, and its type picks the consumer. The in-process Pulsar refuses a second Exclusive consumer at once, so the test fails instead of waiting. Partitions, the key ranges of KeyShared and the consumer a server picks are the server's, and the crate's live tests check them against a running Pulsar.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process Pulsar or against a running server. The service under test charges card payments. A payment arrives on card-payments, and its partition key is the account to charge. The handler replies with a receipt on card-receipts. A payment without a key is dropped. A payment over the bank's instant limit is held: the handler asks for it again in a minute with retry_after. After three deliveries a payment goes to card-payments-review, the dead-letter topic. The app is built by service(broker), so a test chooses the broker and main uses the production one. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-pulsar in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("payments"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } async fn a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let mut key = HeaderMap::new(); key.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, "acct-7"); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .with_headers(key) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, account: "acct-7".to_owned(), }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("payments"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } async fn a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let mut key = HeaderMap::new(); key.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, "acct-7"); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .with_headers(key) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, account: "acct-7".to_owned(), }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start connects PulsarBroker to an in-process Pulsar. The service URL is checked as the client would parse it, and never dialled. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>(). The partition key travels as the PARTITION_KEY_HEADER header, so the test sets it with with_headers. The broker turns that header into the message's key, and the handler reads it back from the same header. publish returns once the handler and its reply have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled and what reached card-receipts. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_without_an_account_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("payments"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 2, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_without_an_account_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("payments"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&Payment { id: 2, amount_cents: 2_500, }) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } settled checks the outcome the handler returned. assert_not_called checks that no receipt was published.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_payment_the_bank_keeps_holding_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("payments"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; let held = Payment { id: 3, amount_cents: 250_000, }; let mut key = HeaderMap::new(); key.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, "acct-7"); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&held) .with_headers(key) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // Each delivery waits `HOLD`, then the broker hands the same message over again. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called(2); // The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows: after its wait, the client // moves the payment to the review topic. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack], ); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments-review") .assert_called_once() .with(&held); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_payment_the_bank_keeps_holding_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let broker = PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("payments"); let tb = TestApp::start(service(broker)).await?; let held = Payment { id: 3, amount_cents: 250_000, }; let mut key = HeaderMap::new(); key.insert(PARTITION_KEY_HEADER, "acct-7"); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .message(&held) .with_headers(key) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // Each delivery waits `HOLD`, then the broker hands the same message over again. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called(2); // The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows: after its wait, the client // moves the payment to the review topic. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack], ); tb.broker::<PulsarBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments-review") .assert_called_once() .with(&held); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } The test starts on a paused clock, and advance moves it forward. A minute of HOLD costs nothing. retry_after holds the payment in the service for the delay and then negatively acknowledges it, so the broker delivers the same message again. Nothing is published for the retry: the test's own payment is the only message on card-payments. The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows, so after its wait the payment goes to card-payments-review as it arrived. Each held delivery is recorded as Outcome::Nack.
