documents.t: The in-process Pulsar reads the configuration a server would get: the broker's settings, each descriptor and the retry declaration of each registration. It refuses what a server refuses, with the error the live broker returns: a service URL the client cannot parse, a destination that is not a topic name, a second consumer of an Exclusive subscription, and a handle used after shutdown. It models Pulsar rather than a queue: A topic is its full name, so orders and persistent://public/default/orders are one topic. Each subscription gets every message of its topics once, and its type picks the consumer. A negatively acknowledged message goes back to its subscription, and the dead-letter policy counts its deliveries as the client does. Each topic keeps its log, so a seek replays it; a non-persistent topic replays nothing. A pattern subscription reads a new topic from the client's next listing, 30 seconds of the paused clock later. Headers travel as text properties, and a payload over max_message_size fails the publish. A server keeps a second Exclusive consumer waiting, while the in-process Pulsar refuses it at once, so such a test fails instead of hanging. The redelivery after the acknowledgement timeout, partitioned topics, the key ranges of KeyShared and messages published while a subscription has no consumer need a server.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt_on_a_server() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = stand() else { return Ok(()); }; let subscription = format!("payments-{}", process::id()); let broker = PulsarBroker::new(url).default_subscription(subscription); let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_keyed_payment_gets_a_receipt_on_a_server() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = stand() else { return Ok(()); }; let subscription = format!("payments-{}", process::id()); let broker = PulsarBroker::new(url).default_subscription(subscription); let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(broker)).await?; a_receipt_names_the_account_of_the_key(tb).await } TestApp::start_live connects the same app to a running Pulsar. The test reads the address from PULSAR_TEST_URL with stand, a helper of the example's own, and skips when it is unset. RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1 turns that skip into a failure, so a CI job cannot pass without the server. The test joins a subscription of its own, named after the process. A new subscription starts at the end of the topic, so nothing an earlier run left behind is read. The assertions are the in-process ones, unchanged. cargo test PULSAR_TEST_URL=pulsar://localhost:6650 cargo test -- --test-threads=1 The server is the one from Getting started.

documents.t: This guide names Pulsar topics, reads them under durable subscriptions, and covers one topic, a fixed list or every topic a pattern matches. The example is a fulfilment service. It ships orders, notifies customers, totals and audits regional orders, and restocks returns.

A Pulsar topic name has four parts: persistent://public/default/orders. The first is the persistence, then come the tenant and the namespace, then the topic itself. A bare name such as orders is short for persistent://public/default/orders, and a tenant/namespace/topic triple is persistent too. public/default is the namespace every Pulsar installation starts with. A persistent topic stores its messages until every subscription has acknowledged them. A non-persistent topic keeps them in memory and hands each one only to the consumers connected at that moment, so it suits data that is worthless a moment later. Pulsar creates a topic on its first use, so a service only names the topics it reads and writes. The service checks every topic name before it connects, and a malformed one stops it at startup. PulsarTopic builds a name from its parts, or parses one that comes from outside the code.

Pulsar reads a topic only through a subscription. A subscription is a cursor the server keeps: it remembers what its consumers acknowledged, and it outlives the service. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Ships every order. The subscription `fulfilment` is this service's cursor on `orders`. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "fulfilment"))] async fn fulfil(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Reads the same topic under a subscription of its own, so it sees every order too. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "notifications"))] async fn notify(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "customer notified"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Ships every order. The subscription `fulfilment` is this service's cursor on `orders`. struct Fulfil; impl Handle<Order> for Fulfil { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Reads the same topic under a subscription of its own, so it sees every order too. struct Notify; impl Handle<Order> for Notify { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "customer notified"); ready(Ok(())) } } PulsarSubscription::new names the topic and the subscription. fulfil and notify read orders under two subscriptions, so each of them gets every order. Two instances of the service share one cursor per subscription, so they split the orders between them instead of shipping each one twice. Name a subscription after the service that owns it: another service that names the same one shares its backlog. A new subscription starts at the end of its topic and sees only what is published after it. An existing one resumes where its consumers stopped, also after a restart. Replay and seeking moves the cursor.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Totals the orders of two regions through one consumer. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::topics(["orders-eu", "orders-us"], "regional-totals"))] async fn tally(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.region, "order counted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Totals the orders of two regions through one consumer. struct Tally; impl Handle<Order> for Tally { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.region, "order counted"); ready(Ok(())) } } PulsarSubscription::topics reads several topics through one consumer, under one subscription name. Each topic keeps its own cursor under that name. All the topics share one payload type.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Audits every regional topic, those created after startup included. #[subscriber(PulsarSubscription::pattern("persistent://public/default/orders-.*", "audit"))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, order.region, "order audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Audits every regional topic, those created after startup included. struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, order.region, "order audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } PulsarSubscription::pattern reads every topic whose full name matches a regular expression, so the expression is written in full. It reads the namespace its prefix names: persistent://acme/orders/.* reads acme/orders, and a pattern with no tenant/namespace/ part reads public/default. audit reads orders-eu and orders-us, and any topic created later whose full name the expression matches. The client lists the topics again every 30 seconds. A new topic is read from the listing that finds it on, and what reached it before that listing is not delivered. An expression that is not a valid regular expression, or whose tenant or namespace is itself a regular expression, stops the service at startup.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Restocks returned items, under the broker's default subscription. #[subscriber("returns")] async fn restock(item: &Return) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(item.order, "return restocked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("fulfilment", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("fulfilment"), |b| { b.include(fulfil); b.include(notify); b.include(tally); b.include(audit); b.include(restock); }, ) } src/main.rs /// Restocks returned items, under the broker's default subscription. struct Restock; impl Handle<Return> for Restock { fn handle( &self, item: &Return, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(item.order, "return restocked"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("fulfilment", "0.1.0")).with_broker( PulsarBroker::new("pulsar://localhost:6650").default_subscription("fulfilment"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "fulfilment"), Fulfil).build()); b.include( subscriber(PulsarSubscription::new("orders", "notifications"), Notify).build(), ); b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::topics(["orders-eu", "orders-us"], "regional-totals"), Tally, ) .build(), ); b.include( subscriber( PulsarSubscription::pattern("persistent://public/default/orders-.*", "audit"), Audit, ) .build(), ); b.include(subscriber("returns", Restock).build()); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } #[subscriber("returns")] names a topic and no subscription. It joins the broker's default_subscription, here fulfilment, as a Shared subscription. A bare name on a broker without a default subscription stops the service at startup, and the error names the setting. Every other setting of a subscription, such as its type or its acknowledgement timeout, needs a descriptor.

The tests in the example file run the app in process. Each subscription over a topic gets every message published to it, as on a server. The pattern test starts on a paused clock and moves it 30 seconds forward with tb.advance, so the next listing comes at once. Testing a Pulsar service covers the harness.
